ai.definition: Swarm Robotic Assembly involves multiple, often identical or similar, autonomous robots working together in a coordinated manner to construct large-scale structures without centralized control.
ai.howItWorks: Robots within the swarm follow decentralized algorithms that allow them to communicate and coordinate their actions. They can sense their environment, detect obstacles, and adjust their movements accordingly to place materials accurately and efficiently.
ai.problemSolved: Efficient construction of complex architectural designs at reduced costs compared to traditional methods and human labor.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves designing the individual robots, developing swarm algorithms, and assembling the hardware and software components. Each robot is typically small and lightweight, allowing for rapid prototyping and scaling.
ai.buildProcess: Robots are deployed in a predefined area where they gather materials from a central supply or source. They then follow pre-programmed or dynamically adjusted paths to place these materials according to the design plan. The swarm algorithms ensure that tasks are distributed efficiently among robots, optimizing resource utilization.
ai.costDrivers: High initial R&D investment for algorithm development and hardware miniaturization; ongoing costs for software updates and maintenance of large-scale systems.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected to transition from prototype testing to early commercial within the next few years, depending on successful field trials and regulatory approvals.
ai.regulation: Currently in a phase where specific regulations are still being defined. Expectations for safety standards, environmental impact assessments, and operational guidelines will be critical as the technology matures.
ai.risks: Technical challenges such as ensuring robust communication between robots, preventing collisions, and handling unpredictable environmental factors; regulatory hurdles related to safety and liability concerns.
ai.profitability: Potential for significant cost savings in construction projects but currently limited by high initial development costs. Expected profitability will depend on the scale of deployment and efficiency improvements over time.
ai.futureDevelopment: Focus areas include improving swarm algorithms, enhancing material handling capabilities, and expanding application domains beyond architecture to other industries such as manufacturing and infrastructure maintenance.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and microfabrication processes. Overall operational power consumption is moderate but varies based on the size and complexity of the structure being built.

glossary.def: Decentralized computational methods that enable multiple robots to coordinate their actions without a central controller.
A system design where decision-making and coordination are distributed among the components rather than centralized in one entity.

subsystems.name: Robots
subsystems.role: small mobile units that pick up, carry and place building elements.

subsystems.name: Communication
subsystems.role: lets robots share local information without a central controller.

subsystems.name: Localisation
subsystems.role: each robot must know its position and that of neighbours and blocks.

subsystems.name: Control software
subsystems.role: decentralised algorithms that turn simple rules into coordinated building.

subsystems.name: Building material
subsystems.role: standardised blocks or components designed for robotic handling.

subsystems.name: Site infrastructure
subsystems.role: provides a known reference frame and power if needed.

buildSteps.title: Design for robotic assembly
buildSteps.detail: The structure is broken into standard modules small enough for a robot to carry, with joints that self-align.

buildSteps.title: Define the building blocks
buildSteps.detail: Blocks are made from lightweight material and given features such as pegs, magnets or grooves so robots can grip and align them.

buildSteps.title: Program the swarm
buildSteps.detail: Each robot runs the same simple rule set: if you see a gap, fetch a block and place it; if blocked, wait or find another task.

buildSteps.title: Set up the site
buildSteps.detail: Localisation beacons or markers are placed so robots can determine their position to within a few centimetres.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Robots are charged, tested and started from a staging area; they synchronise their clocks and maps.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the structure
buildSteps.detail: Robots move to pick up blocks, carry them to the build front, and place them in sequence, using local sensing to align.

buildSteps.title: Inspect and repair
buildSteps.detail: Robots or a separate inspection swarm check for misplacements and correct them before the next layer.

buildSteps.title: Complete and hand over
buildSteps.detail: Once the last block is placed, the swarm is recalled and the structure is verified against the design.

prerequisites.why: lab demonstrations show tens of robots building simple structures, but not at construction scale.
scalable rules exist in simulation, but real-world noise and failures are hard to manage.
indoor and cluttered sites need alternatives such as ultra-wideband or visual markers.
electric motors and lightweight arms are available, but endurance is limited.
radio modules can network hundreds of nodes, but bandwidth and latency must suit real-time control.

pathway.milestone: laboratory swarms build small structures from identical blocks (e.g. Harvard's TERMES project, 2014)
pathway.unlocks: proof that simple local rules can produce complex shapes.

pathway.milestone: outdoor trials with dozens of robots assembling a wall or small shelter
pathway.unlocks: experience with uneven ground, weather and real materials.

pathway.milestone: heterogeneous swarms with specialised robots for carrying, placing and inspecting
pathway.unlocks: faster assembly and ability to handle larger components.

pathway.milestone: construction-site deployment for buildings, or off-world habitats
pathway.unlocks: automated building in places unsafe or impractical for human crews.
